fields.h1: Why Do We Long for Something This World Can’t Give?
fields.meta_title: Why Do We Long for More? The Longing for Heaven
fields.description: That ache at the edge of beauty is not a trick of the nerves. Scripture calls it a homesickness for God — and C. S. Lewis made it the heart of his case for faith. Here is what it means, and what to do with it.
fields.body_html:
Almost everyone knows the feeling. A piece of music, a line of a poem, the smell of rain on a summer road, a view of far hills at evening — and suddenly something aches in you, a longing so sharp it is almost pain, for something you cannot name. It passes in a moment, and leaves you wanting it back. The Bible’s answer is that this longing is not a trick of the nerves or a leftover from childhood. It is a homesickness. You were made for God, and nothing less than God will do.

That answer is very old. But in the last century it was given its best-known modern form by C. S. Lewis, the Oxford scholar who came back to Christian faith from atheism in his early thirties and spent the rest of his life explaining it. This article sets out what Scripture says about that longing, how Lewis understood it, and what to do when it comes.

A longing nothing here can satisfy

The Preacher of Ecclesiastes noticed it three thousand years ago. Having tried every pleasure, every achievement and every kind of wisdom the world could offer, he found that none of them filled the hollow at the centre. And he gave the reason in one of the most remarkable sentences in the Old Testament: God “hath made every thing beautiful in his time: also he hath set the world in their heart, so that no man can find out the work that God maketh from the beginning to the end” (Ecclesiastes 3:11). Many translators render that middle phrase as eternity: God has set eternity in the human heart. We are creatures of time with an appetite for the timeless.

That is why the best things of earth so often leave us wistful rather than satisfied. The holiday ends. The book closes. The friendship, however dear, cannot be all we hoped. Even the moments of greatest happiness seem to point past themselves, like a window rather than a wall. The psalmist knew the feeling and named its true object:

As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God. My soul thirsteth for God, for the living God: when shall I come and appear before God?

Psalm 42:1–2

Augustine of Hippo, four centuries after Christ, put the same truth at the very beginning of his Confessions, in the form of a prayer that has been repeated ever since:

Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee.

Augustine, Confessions

What C. S. Lewis called joy

Lewis knew this longing from early childhood. As a small boy in Belfast he would be ambushed by sudden stabs of desire — at the memory of a toy garden his brother had made in a biscuit tin, at a line of Norse poetry, at the autumn feel of a story. He came to call the experience Joy, and he was careful to distinguish it from happiness or pleasure. Pleasure is something you can have; Joy, as he described it, is something you want, and the wanting is itself strangely precious, more precious than most things you can have.

For years, as an atheist, he chased it. He tried to find it again in books, in landscape, in the imagination, even in the occult, and every time he seemed to grasp it, it was gone. What finally changed him was the realisation that the longing had never really been for any of those things at all. They were the places where it had shown itself, not the thing it was reaching for. When he became a Christian, he found that Joy lost its old importance. It had been like a lit window seen from a dark road: precious while you are outside in the cold, but no longer the point once you are home.

Lewis tells that story in his spiritual autobiography, Surprised by Joy, and he set out the reasoning behind it in Mere Christianity and in his sermon The Weight of Glory. His books are still in copyright, so we will not quote them here; but the shape of the argument is simple enough to put in our own words.

The argument from desire

Lewis observed that, in general, creatures are not born with desires unless something exists to satisfy them. Thirst is real, and so is water. The migrating bird is restless in autumn, and there is a warmer country to fly to. The eye longs for light, and there is a sun. Loneliness aches, and there is such a thing as friendship. The appetite, in each case, fits a real object.

Now suppose we find in ourselves a desire that nothing in this world can satisfy — not because we have been unlucky, but because every earthly good, even at its best, falls short of it. The most reasonable explanation, Lewis argued, is not that the desire is a mistake, but that we were made for another world. Our longing is a clue. It does not by itself prove that heaven is real; but it is exactly what we should expect to feel if Christianity is true, and very hard to make sense of if it is not.

Scripture says the same of the people of faith in every age. Abraham and the patriarchs, says the letter to the Hebrews, “confessed that they were strangers and pilgrims on the earth. For they that say such things declare plainly that they seek a country… But now they desire a better country, that is, an heavenly: wherefore God is not ashamed to be called their God: for he hath prepared for them a city” (Hebrews 11:13–14, 16). Paul tells the Philippians the same: “For our conversation is in heaven; from whence also we look for the Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ” (Philippians 3:20). The citizenship comes first; the homesickness follows.

Three wrong turns

If this longing is real and universal, what do people do with it? Lewis described three common responses, and most of us will recognise ourselves in at least one of them.

The first is to blame the things. We decide that the longing went unsatisfied because we picked the wrong partner, the wrong career, the wrong house, the wrong church. So we try another, and another, always sure that the next one will be the one. This is the restless road of the consumer and the serial romantic, and it ends in exhaustion.

The second is to give up. We conclude, in the name of maturity, that the longing was a youthful illusion. We settle for a sensible, moderate life, expect little, and are rarely disappointed. It looks like wisdom; in fact it is a kind of slow starvation of the soul, the deliberate decision not to be hungry any more.

The third is the Christian way. We accept that earthly goods are real goods — gifts from a generous Father, to be enjoyed with gratitude — but that they were never meant to bear the whole weight of our longing. They are copies, echoes, foretastes. We hold them loosely, thank God for them, and let them turn our faces towards the One they come from. Jesus said it plainly: “Lay not up for yourselves treasures upon earth, where moth and rust doth corrupt… But lay up for yourselves treasures in heaven… For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also” (Matthew 6:19–21).

Longing in a groaning world

The longing is not only for beauty. It is also for justice, for healing, for the end of death. Every hospital ward, every graveside and every news bulletin stirs it. Paul says that the whole creation shares the ache: “For we know that the whole creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together until now. And not only they, but ourselves also, which have the firstfruits of the Spirit, even we ourselves groan within ourselves, waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body” (Romans 8:22–23).

Notice that Christians groan too — perhaps more than anyone, because they know what they are waiting for. Faith does not numb the longing; it sharpens it and gives it a name. The Spirit within us is the “firstfruits,” the first sheaf of a harvest that is certainly coming. And the promise at the end of the Bible is not a vague afterglow but a home: “And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away” (Revelation 21:4).

What to do with the longing

If you know this ache, here are some ways to treat it as a friend rather than a torment.

Name it truthfully. When the stab of longing comes — at a piece of music, a sunset, a child’s laugh — say to yourself, and to God, what it really is. This is not enough, and it was never meant to be. I am made for You. That simple act of naming turns a passing mood into prayer.

Give thanks for the echo. Do not despise earthly beauty because it is not heaven. Enjoy it the more because it is a foretaste. “In thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore” (Psalm 16:11). Every lesser pleasure is a small preview of that fulness.

Set your mind above. “If ye then be risen with Christ, seek those things which are above, where Christ sitteth on the right hand of God. Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth” (Colossians 3:1–2). This is not escapism. Again and again in the church’s history, the men and women who built hospitals, fought slavery and carried the gospel to the ends of the earth were those whose hope was fixed beyond this world. Freed from the desperate need to make earth into heaven, they were free to serve it.

Come to the spring. The longing is, in the end, a thirst, and Jesus offers to meet it Himself: “Whosoever drinketh of this water shall thirst again: but whosoever drinketh of the water that I shall give him shall never thirst; but the water that I shall give him shall be in him a well of water springing up into everlasting life” (John 4:13–14). The deepest desire of the human heart is not for an experience, or even for a place, but for Christ.

Wait in hope. “Beloved, now are we the sons of God, and it doth not yet appear what we shall be: but we know that, when he shall appear, we shall be like him; for we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). The longing will not be fully answered in this life. But it will be answered. “For our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory” (2 Corinthians 4:17).

The longing is a promise

The ache you feel at the edge of beauty is not cruelty. It is kindness. It is God’s way of keeping you from settling for less than Himself, a thread of desire running through every life and leading, if we will follow it, home. Augustine followed it from restlessness to rest. Lewis followed it from atheism to Christ. You can follow it too.

To go further, read the old books in which this longing first found words. Augustine’s Confessions is the classic story of a restless heart finding its rest. John Bunyan’s The Pilgrim’s Progress turns the whole Christian life into a journey to the Celestial City. And for an introduction to Lewis’s thought — summarised, not quoted — see the Ochorus companion The Key Teachings of C. S. Lewis.
